To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the prevalence of elevated hsCRP and/or IL-6 is high in elderly subjects, (ii) the prevalence of high levels of both inflammatory markers is higher in subjects with CVD, (iii) the association between inflammatory markers and CVD in elderly subjects is independent of traditional cardiovascular risk factors and is stronger in women, (iv) elevated hsCRP is a strong and independent predictor of all-cause mortality in elderly subjects, and (v) elevated levels of both markers

the inflammatory markers, hsCRP, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, and sICAM-1, are associated with increased cardiovascular risk in older persons, and that hsCRP is associated with increased mortality in older persons.

1) the association between inflammation and cardiovascular disease (CVD) in the elderly is complex and may be different than in younger adults, 2) the association between CVD risk factors and inflammation is complex and may also be different in the elderly than in younger adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the role of inflammatory markers in the development of cardiovascular disease in elderly people.
the relationship between cardiovascular disease, aging and inflammation.
the study of cardiovascular diseases, particularly atherosclerosis, and the mechanisms by which the disease is initiated and propagated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence for an association between CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α and cardiovascular disease risk in the elderly is weak.
the elderly have an increased risk of CVD, but this is not a result of atherosclerosis.
the elderly have an increased risk for cardiovascular disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the elderly have a different pattern of inflammatory markers than the younger population and that these inflammatory markers are associated with cardiovascular disease.
in elderly people, the presence of cardiovascular disease is associated with a higher level of C-reactive protein (CRP) but not of interleukin-6 (IL-6).
the elderly with a history of cardiovascular disease and/or diabetes have a higher inflammatory burden, which may be associated with increased risk for future cardiovascular disease events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inflammatory marker, CRP, is not a good marker of cardiovascular disease in elderly patients.
there is a strong link between inflammation and cardiovascular disease, which is not surprising given what is known about the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis.
inflammation may play a role in cardiovascular disease (CVD) in the elderly, and that this role is independent of the presence of atherosclerosis.
